opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a really interesting idea, and I have somewhat mixed feelings about it. The appeal is clear: if you could find some intrinsic measure of how much "stuff" a task requires, like the minimum number of meaningful actions or decisions you have to get right, that would give you a more principled axis than what we've been using. In our time-horizon work, we measure task difficulty by how long it takes a skilled human to do the task. That's useful because it's interpretable and it connects to economic value, but it's also clearly a proxy. Human time bundles together a lot of things, like typing speed, reading speed, how much background knowledge you need to load in, and how much of the task is just waiting for things to run.

So an action count could, in principle, strip some of that away and get closer to the underlying structure of the task. If you think about why longer tasks are harder for models, one natural story is that each step has some chance of going wrong, errors compound, and the model has to notice and recover from mistakes. That story is really about the number of steps, not wall-clock time. So if action count tracked model success better than human time does, that would tell us something about the mechanism.

The hard part is that "intrinsic number of actions" is surprisingly slippery to define. What counts as an action? Is it a keystroke, a shell command, a function call, a high-level decision like "decide which approach to take"? Those vary by orders of magnitude depending on granularity, and the right granularity probably differs between humans and models, and between models with different scaffolds. A model that can write a 200-line file in one tool call is taking "one action" in one sense, but that action contains a huge number of decisions. And actions aren't equally hard. Some are trivial and some carry most of the difficulty of the task. So I'd worry that a naive count ends up noisier than human time, which at least implicitly weights steps by how much thought they need.

Where I think it could be really valuable is as a complementary measure. If you had both human time and some action-based measure, you could look at where they come apart. Tasks that take a long time but need few decisions, versus tasks that are short but very decision-dense, and see which predicts model performance better. That would help us figure out what's actually driving the trend we see, and whether extrapolating it makes sense. So I'm excited about it as a research direction. I just don't think it would cleanly replace human-time-based metrics anytime soon.

r001.rationale: It says each step may go wrong and errors can compound, but does not clearly connect action count to a constant hazard rate model.

r002.rationale: It identifies the difficulty of defining and counting actions, including granularity differences and unequal action difficulty, as limitations of the measure.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's a really natural thing to want to measure, and I think it's useful, but with some pretty important caveats.

The appeal is obvious. If you're trying to characterize what models can and can't do, "how long is the task" is one of the first things you reach for. And the thing that I think METR's time-horizon work got right is that it anchors to something external, like how long it takes a human. The intrinsic number of actions is sort of a cousin of that. Instead of wall-clock time for a human, you're asking: what's the minimum number of discrete steps any reasonable agent would need to take to actually get this done? How many commands do you have to run, how many files do you have to edit, how many things do you have to look at before you can even know what to do.

The reason I like it as a frame is that it gets at something real about the failure mode we see with agents. A lot of the time the model isn't failing because any individual step is hard. It's failing because there are forty steps and at step twenty-three it does something slightly wrong and never recovers, or it loses track of what it was doing. So a task that has a high intrinsic action count is stressing a different capability than a task that's a single hard reasoning problem you can answer in one shot. Separating those out seems valuable. If you only look at "percent of tasks solved," you're mashing together "can it do the hard thing" and "can it stay coherent over a long trajectory."

The caveats, though. The first one is that "intrinsic" is doing a lot of work in that phrase. The minimum number of actions depends enormously on what you count as an action and what tools you give the agent. If I give you a shell, a task might be thirty actions. If I give you a tool that does the whole thing in one call, it's one action. So it's not really a property of the task, it's a property of the task plus the affordances, and you have to be careful not to pretend it's more objective than it is.

The second thing is that the minimum path is often not the path anyone actually takes, humans included. A good engineer solving a problem does a lot of exploratory actions that aren't strictly necessary in hindsight. So if you measure the shortest possible path, you might be measuring something that doesn't correspond to how hard the task actually feels to do. And models in particular tend to take way more actions than the minimum, so the gap between intrinsic actions and actual actions is itself interesting, maybe more interesting than the intrinsic number alone.

And then the third thing is that action count doesn't capture how much is riding on each action. Some tasks have a hundred steps where any error is recoverable, and some have five steps where if you get step two wrong you're done. Those feel very different in terms of what capability they're testing, and a raw count flattens that.

So my honest take is: useful as one axis, probably best alongside something like human time and some notion of how recoverable errors are, and I'd be wary of anyone presenting it as the number that explains agent capability. But I do think it's pointing at the right phenomenon, which is that length-of-trajectory is a distinct thing from difficulty-of-individual-step, and we should measure them separately.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses action count as a capability measure but does not connect it to a constant hazard rate model.

r002.rationale: The candidate says the minimum action count depends heavily on what counts as an action and which tools are available, making it difficult to treat as an objective task property.

astra-6.text:
I think it could be useful, but I’m not sure there’s a well-defined intrinsic number of actions for most tasks. It depends on what you count as an action and what tools the system has access to. Something that takes a hundred actions in one interface might take one action in another, even though we’d intuitively consider it the same task.

There’s also a distinction between how many actions you need to execute a solution and how difficult it is to find that solution. You could have a problem where the final answer is just one choice, but figuring out which choice to make requires a lot of reasoning. So action count alone would miss an important part of capability.

But if you fix the environment and the available actions, I think it becomes a useful measure of how long a system can reliably pursue a goal. Can it carry out a sequence of dependent steps, notice when something goes wrong, and recover? That seems worth measuring. I’d just treat it as one dimension of capability, rather than a general measure of how difficult a task is.

r001.rationale: The response discusses action counts as a possible measure, but does not connect them to a constant hazard rate model.

r002.rationale: It says there may be no well-defined intrinsic action count because what counts as an action depends on the tools and interface, identifying operationalization as a limitation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a useful lens, but I’m not sure there’s a single intrinsic number of actions for a task. It depends on what you count as an action and what tools the system has. Something that takes a person a hundred steps might be one API call for an AI.

But if you fix the interface, then the length of the task does seem important. A system can be very good at individual steps and still struggle to complete a long task, because mistakes accumulate, or because it doesn’t notice when it needs to change its plan. So measuring how performance changes with the number of steps could tell us something that short, isolated questions don’t.

I’d want to distinguish that from difficulty, though. There are very hard problems where the answer is a single action, and very long tasks where each action is straightforward. I think those are different dimensions of capability, and we’d like evaluations that capture both.

r001.rationale: The response discusses step length and accumulating mistakes, but does not connect task actions to a constant hazard rate model.

r002.rationale: It says there may be no single intrinsic action count because the count depends on what qualifies as an action and which tools or interface are available.
